Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then: (a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and $\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and $c>0$; its components are the laboratory time coordinate $t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the laboratory position $r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. (b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice $U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the coordinates of $r$ are expressed. (c) [Laboratory fields] A laboratory field of rank $m$ is a map $F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$, $p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class $C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed $t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is asserted beyond the class stated for it. (d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer field is defined here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. (a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$ carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted (the pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical estimate/uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$ or a current measured value); the electric constant is defined within the framework by $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$, so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$. (b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the charge density $\rho$ of [[def-em-sources]] carries C m$^{-3}$ and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where $1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$ carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic two-form of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] carry T; a force carries the newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$. (c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram (kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ carries kg m s$^{-1}$ ([[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]); field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$. (d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI, they do not by themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light, which is the physical adoption of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]].

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is not asserted. (b) [Smooth source fields] A smooth (volume) source field on $\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the frame charge density (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the frame current density (A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if $V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define $Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$ by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf1_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$
where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is defined through its positive and negative parts ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). This integral is absolutely finite, since $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on $\overline V$ and $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure. On the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption, $Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]. The empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal field $n_S$ the current flux at time $t$ is $\int_S J(y,t)\cdot n_S(y)\,dS$ ([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]). Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them. (c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and $j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model, and hence the component transformation law of [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts. This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents. (d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch] Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a $C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier $\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so $u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic convention is $j^0=c\rho$,
$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$
Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$, including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike $U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is $v^i:=cu^i$.
For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch, $U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and
$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$
Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model: in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$ (equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are retained. (e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let $\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative $\partial_t$ at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on $I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as distributional derivatives, and let $\psi$ range over $C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]). Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the pairings $\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle$, $\langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle$, $\langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle$ and $\langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$ vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]). (c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of inertial frame.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

For $a\in\Omega$, the **Dirac distribution at $a$** is the complex-linear functional $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, with the bilinear convention of [[def-distribution]]. It is continuous: the seminorm $q(\varphi)=|\varphi(a)|$ restricts on each $\mathcal D_K$ to a seminorm bounded by $p_0$ (and is zero if $a\notin K$), so it is one of the admissible seminorms defining the test topology.

Its derivatives are those of [[def-distributional-derivative]]:
$$\langle\partial^\alpha\delta_a,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\varphi(a).$$
They are distributions by that definition; on each fixed-support stage the absolute value is at most $p_{|\alpha|}(\varphi)$. If $a\notin K$ all derivatives of the test vanish at $a$, so the bound has zero left side. For $\alpha=0$ this is $\delta_a$; a first derivative evaluates the negative first derivative of the test. No conjugation and no choice are involved. On the empty open set there is no permitted point $a$, rather than a new Dirac distribution. The sharp order of these distributions requires a test witness and is proved in the assigned example later.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$, and put $\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS$ for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, the surface integral being that of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. A continuous density $a$ on $S$ defines $a\delta_S(\psi)=\int_S a\psi\,dS$. Both functionals are continuous of finite order on test functions, because $\lvert a\rvert$ and $\psi$ are bounded on the compact interface and the surface measure is finite. A field that is $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided continuous traces has locally integrable components; write $[F]:=F_+-F_-$ for the jump across $S$.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

supplier_pins.exact_interface: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ a $C^1$ trajectory, and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ open containing its graph. Assume the graph map $\gamma:I\to\Omega$, $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$, is proper: the inverse image of every compact subset of $\Omega$ is compact in $I$. For $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ define $\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ and $\langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_I z'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$. These define distributions and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. Properness is automatic if $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, or if $I=\mathbb R$. Endpoint variant: if $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite, and both endpoint events belong to $\Omega$, the same integrals instead define distributions with $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\delta_{(z(a),a)}-q\delta_{(z(b),b)}$. A finite-history source is source-free only when the endpoint contribution vanishes on the chosen test domain; neither mere graph containment nor test compactness alone supplies this.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

supplier_pins.exact_interface: Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An electric field of class $C^k$ on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a magnetic field of class $C^k$ is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses: $C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and no regularity beyond it is asserted. Conventions: (a) $E$ is a polar vector and $B$ an axial vector relative to the orientation of the spatial basis; the changes of inertial description adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] are proper and orientation preserving, so orientation-reversing descriptions are not among them; (b) the fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at a point of singular source support is asserted; (c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T; (d) the identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] and is not presupposed here.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

supplier_pins.exact_interface:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

In the flat classical laboratory model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the positive constants and SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]], adopt the following additional physical assumption for models using the declared point or stationary-sheet sources: the locally integrable field pair and the volume-plus-singular source pair of [[def-em-weak-sources]](a)-(d) must satisfy its solution predicate (e). Explicitly,
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$
are required in $\mathcal D'(U)$, meaning that all four residual pairings defined there vanish for every compact smooth test. This is a physical adoption of the classical vacuum idealization in that source class, not a theorem about sources or a consequence of the original locally-integrable-source branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. When the singular part vanishes, the adopted identities coincide with that earlier weak branch.
Only source/field tuples satisfying these identities are models of this postulate; it does not assert existence for every prescribed source pair, and compatibility conditions remain consequences to be checked. Sources are the exact point and stationary-sheet types defined earlier, including their properness/endpoint and tangential-current qualifications. No moving sheet, line current, magnetic source, product of distributions, self-force, regularization, matter dynamics or material constitutive law is introduced. This postulate reports no experiment or measurement and does not infer empirical certainty from its mathematical formulation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the surface-measure interface inherited from [[def-em-surface-distribution]] ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\mathcal D'(U)$ be the space of distributions on $U$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]); recall that the pairing $\langle T,\psi\rangle$ is bilinear with no conjugation and that the distributional partial derivatives are $\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$ ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(a) [Fields as distributions] Locally integrable fields and source densities on $U$ are identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

(b) [Point sources] Let $I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $z:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ trajectory whose graph map $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$ is proper into the open set $U$, and let $q\in\mathbb R$ (coulombs). By [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]],
$$\langle\rho_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}z'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$$
define distributions on $U$ with $\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=0$. If instead $I_0=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite and both endpoint events lie in $U$, the same formulas define distributions with
$$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=q\,\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\,\delta_{\gamma(b)}$$
([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); a finite-history point source therefore contributes an endpoint term unless that term is included explicitly, and the pairings above exclude it only by the stated properness or endpoint hypotheses.

(c) [Stationary-sheet sources] Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]), and let $\sigma:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous with $K(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a tangential surface current density; the sheet is stationary). Then
$$\langle\rho_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_S\sigma(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_SK(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt$$
define distributions on $U$: for $\psi$ with compact support the inner integrals are continuous in $t$ on a compact parameter interval and the functionals are bounded by $(\sup|\sigma\psi|)\,\mathrm{area}(S)\,\mathrm{length}$ of the time projection of the support, and likewise in the vector case. A normal sheet current (one with $K\cdot n\ne0$), a line current and a moving sheet are not source types of this definition.

(d) [Unrestricted weak fields and optional interface branches] The general field class for the solution predicate (e) consists of all locally integrable pairs $(E,B)$ on $U$, also when the source has a stationary-sheet part. No classical one-sided trace or off-sheet $C^1$ regularity is required to define those four distributional pairings. Additional trace hypotheses are optional hypotheses of interface/jump results, not admission requirements of the general weak model.
For a pointwise classical jump branch, one may additionally assume that $E,B$ are $C^1$ off $S\times I$ and, around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighborhood of the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder. These joint one-sided extensions make the field traces and first spatial/temporal derivatives continuous up to that side, locally uniformly on compact cylinders.
For the broader weak-trace branch, one may instead assume the original one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time, with the explicit additional conditions that the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the field traces are measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ for $dSdt$. This branch supports sheet-distribution and almost-everywhere jump identities; spatial continuity at each time gives pointwise spatial identities for almost every time, and joint continuity of the jump densities gives the further all-time upgrade. Separate spatial $C^1$ traces at each time alone do not imply that joint regularity or upgrade. Whenever such traces exist, $[F]:=F_+-F_-$ denotes their jump in the chosen normal convention. (e) [Weak Maxwell equations with a distributional source pair] Let $E,B$ be a field pair of class (d), let $\rho=\rho_v+\rho_s$ and $J=J_v+J_s$ be source distributions on $U$ whose volume parts $\rho_v,J_v$ are locally integrable volume densities with the charge/current quantity types of [[def-em-sources]] (the weak predicate requires this stated $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ regularity, not the classical continuous-source regularity) and whose singular parts $(\rho_s,J_s)$ are point sources as in (b) or stationary-sheet sources as in (c), and let $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Say that $E,B$ satisfy the weak Maxwell equations with the source pair $(\rho,J)$ when, for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, the four pairings
$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$
all vanish, all derivatives being distributional derivatives of the regular distributions of the fields and the source pairings being those of (b) and (c). This clause defines a solution predicate. When the singular parts vanish, its four identities are the same as the locally integrable weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. That earlier postulate explicitly excludes point and sheet distributions and does not imply their physical adoption here; adoption for the declared singular-source models is made separately, after this definition. No physical field equation is deduced merely from defining this predicate.

(f) [Scope] No product of two distributions is formed anywhere: the fields occur only through their distributional derivatives paired with a test function, and the source densities $\sigma,K$ occur only inside the ordinary surface and time integrals of (b) and (c); products such as $\rho_sE$ or $J_s\times B$ are not defined by this item. The definition asserts no existence theorem for fields with singular sources, no conservation law (continuity for these sources is proved separately where used), and no regularisation. Sources that are not locally integrable and are not point or stationary-sheet sources, moving sheets, line currents, and arbitrary products of distributions are outside the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $S\subset\Omega$ be a two-sided compact embedded $C^2$ interface with unit normal $n$ from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, and let $F$ be $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided $C^1$ traces on $S$. Then, away from the edge $\partial S$ and in the distributional sense, $$\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S,\qquad \operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[F]\,\delta_S,$$ where the bracket terms denote the locally integrable functions equal to the classical divergence and curl on each open side and $[F]=F_+-F_-$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the surface-measure interface cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], and let $a:S\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. If $\int_Sa\psi\,dS=0$ for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]), then $a=0$ on $S$. Equivalently, if two continuous densities on $S$ pair equally against every test function, they are equal pointwise on $S$. The conclusion is pointwise and uses the continuity of $a$; a merely locally integrable density would satisfy only an almost-everywhere conclusion, which this statement does not claim.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge1$ there is a fixed smooth $b:\mathbb R^n\to[0,1]$, equal to one on $\overline B_1(0)$ and with support contained in $B_2(0)$. For $a\in\mathbb R^n,r>0$, $b_{a,r}(x)=b((x-a)/r)$ satisfies $\int|Db_{a,r}|=C_nr^{n-1}$, where $C_n=\int|Db|<\infty$. For every $0<r<R$ one can instead obtain a smooth bump equal to one on $\overline B_r(a)$ and supported strictly inside $B_R(a)$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants and units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E,B$ be the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and $\rho,J$ the source fields of [[def-em-sources]], with $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly of class $C^2$ on $\Omega\times I$ and $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$, and suppose the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds with these fields and sources, in particular $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$. Then the continuity equation
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$$
holds pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, where $\operatorname{div}$ is the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and $\partial_t$ the partial time derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

(b) [Distributional branch] Let $E,B,\rho,J$ be distributions on $\Omega\times I$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]); in particular they may be locally integrable fields and sources identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Suppose the four equations
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$
hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega\times I)$ with distributional derivatives. This includes the original locally integrable weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and the separately adopted declared singular-source models of [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], when their source/field hypotheses hold. More generally the formal compatibility implication applies to every distributional source pair for which the four identities hold, without asserting physical adoption of arbitrary distributions. Then
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$$
in $\mathcal D'(\Omega\times I)$.

The conclusion is a compatibility condition: it does not assert that every source pair is compatible with the Maxwell equations, and by itself it proves no conservation of physical charge. The derivative compatibility argument is choice-free. An application to the declared singular-source model retains the Countable Choice assumption of its defining source/surface-measure formulation ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

supplier_pins.exact_interface:
Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is

measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

supplier_pins.exact_interface:
Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

before_object.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]), inherited from [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]]. Let $t_0<T$ be real, let $E_0,B_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^\infty$ fields ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) on the whole-space laboratory region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and assume the constraints $$\operatorname{div}E_0=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B_0=0$$ on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Put $\dot E_0:=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$ and $\dot B_0:=-\operatorname{curl}E_0$. No decay, boundedness, compactness or finite-energy hypothesis is imposed on the data. Then: (a) [Existence and explicit representation] There are jointly $C^\infty$ fields $E,B:\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R^3$ (in the extension sense of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]]) satisfying the four smooth-branch vacuum Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$, $J\equiv0$ and the initial conditions $E(\cdot,t_0)=E_0$, $B(\cdot,t_0)=B_0$, $\partial_tE(\cdot,t_0)=\dot E_0$, $\partial_tB(\cdot,t_0)=\dot B_0$. Explicitly, each component $E_i$ is the scalar solution $u$ of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](a) with data $(a,b)=(E_{0,i},\dot E_{0,i})$ and $h=0$, each $B_i$ that with $(a,b)=(B_{0,i},\dot B_{0,i})$, in the spherical-mean representation $u=\partial_sH_a+H_b$ of that theorem (the mean being that of [[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]]). (b) [Uniqueness] Every pair of jointly $C^2$ fields on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ (in the extension sense) satisfying the same four equations with $\rho\equiv0$, $J\equiv0$ and $E'(\cdot,t_0)=E_0$, $B'(\cdot,t_0)=B_0$ equals $(E,B)$; the time derivatives at $t_0$ are then automatically $\dot E_0,\dot B_0$ by the Ampere and Faraday equations. (c) [Finite propagation and domain of dependence] If a second pair of constrained data $(E_0',B_0')$ agrees with $(E_0,B_0)$ together with all curls on the closed ball $\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$ — that is, $E_0=E_0'$, $B_0=B_0'$, $\operatorname{curl}E_0=\operatorname{curl}E_0'$ and $\operatorname{curl}B_0=\operatorname{curl}B_0'$ there — then the corresponding solutions agree at $(x_*,t_*)$, for all $x_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and $t_*\in[t_0,T]$. Consequently the value at $(x_*,t_*)$ is determined by the Cauchy data on the closed backward cone $K(x_*,t_*)=\{(y,v):|y-x_*|\le c(t_*-v)\}$ of [[def-forward-and-backward-wave-cones-domain-of-dependence-and-influence]]. In the causal geometry of the adopted affine Minkowski model this cone is the model's causal past cone of the event $(x_*,t_*)$ in the chart $x^0=ct$; by the reachability objects of [[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]] and the straight-segment criterion and time monotonicity of [[thm-sr-future-cone-and-flat-domain-of-dependence]], events outside it cannot be joined to $(x_*,t_*)$ by a future causal path, so the constructed field supplies no vacuum influence outside the model's causal cones; this identification of the PDE cone with the model's causal cone is the modelling statement of the item, not an additional empirical claim. (d) [Compact support] If in addition $E_0$ and $B_0$ vanish off a compact set $K\subset\mathbb R^3$, choose $\rho>0$ with $K\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$ ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]); then for every $t\in[t_0,T]$ one has $E(x,t)=B(x,t)=0$ whenever $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$. (e) [Scope] This is the smooth whole-space vacuum branch with initially constraint-satisfying data; no finite-total-energy conclusion is drawn (a general smooth but non-decaying solution may have infinite total energy), and no boundary condition, inhomogeneous source, weak-branch content or empirical claim is asserted. The result is conditional on the adopted postulates and on $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the latter used only through the cited scalar theorem.
before_object.strategy: Set $\dot E_0=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$, $\dot B_0=-\operatorname{curl}E_0$, and solve the six scalar Cauchy problems by [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](a) with data $(E_{0,i},\dot E_{0,i})$ and $(B_{0,i},\dot B_{0,i})$; the $C^\infty$ claim and the explicit representation through the spherical-mean family $H_\varphi=sM_{cs}\varphi$ are clause (a) of that theorem, whose mean is that of [[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]]. Put $R_i:=\partial_tE_i-c^2(\operatorname{curl}B)_i$ and $Q_i:=\partial_tB_i+(\operatorname{curl}E)_i$. Each is $C^\infty$ and solves the homogeneous scalar wave equation: differentiating the component wave equations and commuting derivatives ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]) gives $\partial_t^2R_i=c^2\Delta R_i$, $\partial_t^2Q_i=c^2\Delta Q_i$. Initially $R=Q=0$, and $\partial_tR_i(t_0)=c^2\Delta E_{0,i}+c^2(\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E_0)_i=c^2\nabla_i\operatorname{div}E_0=0$, $\partial_tQ_i(t_0)=c^2\nabla_i\operatorname{div}B_0=0$ by the curl-curl identity [[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]] and the constraints. The uniqueness clause [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](b) applied to the zero wave problem gives $R=Q=0$, i.e. the two evolution equations. The constructed fields are smooth and satisfy the evolution equations with $\operatorname{div}E(\cdot,t_0)=\operatorname{div}E_0=0$ and $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t_0)=0$, so the constraint propagation of [[pthm-em-gauss-constraint-propagation]](a) with $\rho=J=0$ gives $\operatorname{div}E\equiv\operatorname{div}B\equiv0$; all four Maxwell equations therefore hold. Uniqueness (b): any other $C^2$ solution has componentwise the same Cauchy data and, by [[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]], satisfies the homogeneous scalar wave equation, so [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](b) identifies it with the constructed field. Clause (c) applies [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](c) componentwise, whose hypothesis is agreement of both scalar data functions on the ball: $E_0$ and $c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$ for the $E$ components, $B_0$ and $-\operatorname{curl}E_0$ for the $B$ components, exactly the stated hypothesis; the cone reformulation uses the backward-cone object and the causal reachability and future-causal-path conclusions of the two cited SR items as the model's geometric language. Clause (d) applies [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](d) to each component, whose data vanish off $K$ because $E_0,B_0$ and their curls do. No decay or extra regularity is assumed, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is consumed only inside the cited scalar theorem.
before_object.physical_scope: Conditional whole-space smooth-branch vacuum Maxwell initial-value theory in a named inertial chart with SI constants: existence, uniqueness, finite propagation speed $c$ and compact-support propagation for initially constraint-satisfying $C^\infty$ data of arbitrary growth. Excluded: non-smooth and weak-branch data, sources, boundary conditions, finite-domain problems, finite-total-energy or decay conclusions and any empirical claim. $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is declared and used only through the cited scalar wave theorem.

before_object.title: The steady-current (magnetostatic) regime, the compact smooth current class and the declared ideal noncompact models
before_object.statement:
Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(a) [Steady-current regime] A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

(b) [Compact smooth current class] The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

(c) [Declared ideal noncompact models] The framework declares three ideal current models outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields. (c1) [Closed thin loop] For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution $$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$ with $\rho_\gamma:=0$. (c2) [Infinite straight wire] For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is $\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds$, with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$. (c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet] For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is $\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support. (c4) [Admissibility] A field $B$ is admitted for one of these declared models when: $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ (hence a distribution by [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $C^1$ off the support of the current; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ hold pointwise off that support; the distributional identities $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold against every test field $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]; $B$ has the model's declared symmetry (invariance under translations along and rotations about the axis in (c2) and (c3); no symmetry is required in (c1)); and $B$ obeys the decay requirement: $|B(x)|\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in (c1), and in (c2), (c3) the supremum of $|B|$ over every compact set of cross-sectional parameters tends to $0$ as the transverse radius $\rho\to\infty$. The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

(d) [Scope] This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the distributional magnetostatic equations of the declared models are themselves part of the declared model, in the explicitly adopted manner of the framework's singular-source postulate [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], and no product of distributions is formed.
before_object.strategy: **Scope.** A formulation definition with three verifications. (a) is algebra inside the smooth branch: setting $\partial_tE=\partial_tB=\partial_t\rho=\partial_tJ=0$ in the four equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] leaves the displayed pairs, and [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] applied to a steady configuration gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$; no new analysis is claimed. (b) records the exact hypothesis class used by [[pthm-em-magnetostatic-vector-potential]], [[pthm-em-biot-savart]] and [[pthm-em-magnetic-dipole-field]]. (c1)-(c3) define the pairings: for compactly supported $\psi$ the integrals range over the compact sets $\gamma^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\psi)$, the compact intersection of the axis with the $x_3$-projection of $\operatorname{supp}\psi$, or the compact set $S\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi$, so each functional is a finite integral of a continuous function and defines a distribution ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]]). (c4) states what the companion examples verify: the wire and sheet pairings are computed in [[ex-em-infinite-wire-and-solenoid]] using [[lem-em-ideal-line-current-field]] and [[lem-em-ideal-cylindrical-sheet-field]], and the loop field away from the wire is supplied by the thin-current limit of [[lem-em-thin-current-limit]]. The distributional magnetostatic equations of the declared models are adopted here in the same explicitly declared manner as the framework's singular-source postulate [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]]; no product of distributions is formed, since every pairing is between a distribution and a smooth compact test. (d) records the exclusions. The declared symmetry and decay data are part of the model, not derived: the transverse decay excludes an added homogeneous field in (c2) and (c3), and the source term in the distributional equation fixes the remaining normalisation of the models.

before_object.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis under which [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] and the surface conventions of [[def-em-weak-sources]] are stated, and let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]]), let $\sigma_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous with $K_f(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a free surface charge density and a tangential free surface current density, both stationary in $t$), and let $\rho_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $J_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous and locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$. Let $E,B,D,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$ and of class $C^1$ on $(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$, with the joint one-sided $C^1$ extension property: around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side of each field is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder, so that the fields and their first space and time derivatives extend continuously to that side, locally uniformly on compact cylinders. Write $[F]=F_+-F_-$ for the jump of the one-sided traces.
[Thin-interface hypothesis] Suppose that $E,B,D,H$ satisfy the four macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] in the distributional sense on $U$ with the source pair $\rho_f=\rho_v+\sigma_f\delta_S$, $J_f=J_v+K_f\delta_S$, where the stationary-sheet pairings are those of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) and the equations are $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ as identities in the sense of [[def-distribution]], the fields being identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\psi$ ranging over $C_c^\infty(U)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). This thin-interface solution hypothesis is a modelling assumption of the statement: it is the natural weakening of the smooth macroscopic equations to fields with a common stationary discontinuity, and it is not deduced from the smooth-region equations alone.
Then, pointwise on $S\times I$, $$n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f,\qquad n\cdot[B]=0,\qquad n\times[E]=0,\qquad n\times[H]=K_f,$$ with the Euclidean inner and cross products of the one-sided traces ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); equivalently $\sigma_f=n\cdot[D]$ and $K_f=n\times[H]$ recover the free sheet densities from the field jumps.
[Weak-trace branch] If instead of the joint extension hypothesis the fields have the original one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time and, in addition, the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the one-sided field traces are measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ with respect to $dS\,dt$, then the same four identities hold as identities of sheet distributions and for $dS\,dt$-almost every $(x,t)$; since the traces are spatially continuous at each fixed time, they hold for every $x\in S$ for almost every $t$, and at every $(x,t)$ whenever the jump densities are additionally jointly continuous. Merely having one-sided spatial $C^1$ traces separately at every time does not justify the last upgrade.
[Scope] The interface is stationary, so the one-sided $C^1$ traces also make $\partial_tD$ and $\partial_tB$ locally bounded near $S$ and hence locally integrable, contributing no delta terms. No magnetic charge and no magnetic surface current are present in the sources; no dipolar sheet layer (a concentrated dipole distribution in $P$ or $M$, which would make the fields non-integrable) is included. No existence theorem for fields with singular sources is asserted, no constitutive law is used, and no empirical claim is made.

Substituting into the distributional identities of the hypothesis and using the sheet pairings of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c), the regular parts reproduce the off-interface macroscopic equations and the coefficients of $\delta_S$ give, one equation at a time, $n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f$ (from $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$), $n\cdot[B]=0$ (from $\operatorname{div}B=0$), $n\times[E]=0$ and $n\times[H]=K_f$: the right-hand sides $\partial_tB$ and $J_f+\partial_tD$ carry no delta term because $S$ is stationary and the joint one-sided $C^1$ hypothesis makes $\partial_tB$ and $\partial_tD$ locally bounded near $S$, hence locally integrable. Since the two-sided traces are continuous on $S\times I$, the distributional coefficient identities are the displayed pointwise identities. The weak-trace branch replaces the pointwise trace argument by the $dS\,dt$-almost-everywhere sheet identity plus the spatial-continuity upgrade. Thus the fields and their first space/time derivatives extend continuously to that side of $S\times I$, locally uniformly on compact cylinders, and let $\rho_v,J_v$ be continuous on $(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$ and locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$. $$\rho=\rho_v+\rho_S,\qquad J=J_v+J_S,$$
where $(\rho_S,J_S)$ is the stationary-sheet source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) with densities $\sigma,K$ and the pairings there, in the sense of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e), and where the volume parts $\rho_v,J_v$ are identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). The theorem assumes a stationary interface: the hypersurface $S$ and its normal do not depend on $t$, so the one-sided $C^1$ traces also make $\partial_tE$ and $\partial_tB$ locally bounded near $S$ and hence locally integrable, contributing no delta terms. $$\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E,\qquad\partial_tE=c^2\operatorname{curl}B-c^2\mu_0J,$$
and, separately, source continuity $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. No Gauss constraint is assumed. Then $\partial_tD_B=\partial_tD_E=0$ pointwise. For each fixed $x$, both defects are constant on $I$. Initial zero constraints at any $t_0\in I$ persist at every time; a nonzero defect at a point persists with the same value. Thus evolution and continuity cannot repair a nonzero initial Gauss defect.
(b) Distributional evolution branch. The same derivative conclusion holds for arbitrary scalar/vector distributions $E,B,\rho,J$ on $U$ satisfying the two evolution identities and, independently, continuity in $\mathcal D'(U)$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). This includes the original locally integrable field/source branch identified with regular distributions and the declared singular-source class when its equations hold. Thus $\partial_tD_B=\partial_tD_E=0$ distributionally. If a defect has a continuous representative $h$ on $U$, assume Countable Choice for the indicated Lebesgue integral/localization interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); then $h(x,t)$ is independent of $t$. before_object.title: A suddenly appearing point charge with zero current is inadmissible
before_object.statement:
Let $q\ne0$ be a real charge parameter (coulombs) and let $U:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ with the laboratory conventions of [[def-em-weak-sources]]. Define a distribution $\rho$ on $U$ by
$$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle:=q\int_0^\infty\psi(0,t)\,dt,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$$
— an explicit switched-history distribution for $z(t)=0$ on $(0,\infty)$, with no compensating current or source contribution at the appearance event; it does not satisfy the proper-graph hypothesis of the zero-endpoint continuity branch of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) — and let $J:=0$ be the zero distribution. Then:

(a) $\partial_t\rho=q\,\delta_{(0,0)}$ and $\operatorname{div}J=0$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]), hence $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\,\delta_{(0,0)}\ne0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$: for every test function $\psi$, $\langle\partial_t\rho,\psi\rangle=-q\int_0^\infty\partial_t\psi(0,t)\,dt=q\,\psi(0,0)$, because $t\mapsto\psi(0,t)$ is smooth with compact support. In particular the continuity identity fails at the appearance event $(0,0)$.

(b) Consequently there are no locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $U$ satisfying the weak Maxwell equations with the source pair $(\rho,0)$ in the sense of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e): such fields would satisfy the distributional continuity identity of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]](b), which (a) contradicts. The source pair $(\rho,0)$ is therefore incompatible even with the formal four residual identities, and cannot be an actual source/field model under [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]].

(c) The failure is exactly the omitted endpoint term of the point-source construction: by the endpoint clause of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]], the same trajectory on a bounded interval $I_0=(a,b)$ has $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\,\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\,\delta_{\gamma(b)}$ with $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$. before_object.title: Surface independence of the total current flux and the role of the displacement term
before_object.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the test-geometry and divergence-theorem items cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $E,B$ be jointly of class $C^2$ fields of [[def-em-fields]] and $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$ source fields of [[def-em-sources]] satisfying the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on a neighbourhood of the data below.

Suppose given two patch test geometries $(D,r_1)$, $(D,r_2)$ of [[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]] over the same finite elementary Green region $D$ whose induced boundary chains coincide as oriented paths (so both patches span the same closed loop $\gamma$), and suppose there is a bounded open region $V\subseteq\Omega$ with a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation whose boundary faces are exactly the two images $r_1[D]$, $r_2[D]$ with outward normals $-n_1$ and $+n_2$ respectively, where $n_i$ is the normal induced by $r_i$ (that is, $V$ is the region enclosed between the two patches; this is a hypothesis on the pair, part of its data). Then, for every $t\in I$:

(a) [Total current flux is surface independent]
$$\int_{S_1}\bigl(J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE\bigr)(\cdot,t)\cdot n_1\,dS=\int_{S_2}\bigl(J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE\bigr)(\cdot,t)\cdot n_2\,dS=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\oint_\gamma B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r,$$
where $S_i=r_i[D]$ and the flux is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

(b) [Conduction-only flux need not be] For every $t\in I$ the difference of the conduction fluxes equals the negative of the difference of the displacement fluxes:
$$\int_{S_1}J(\cdot,t)\cdot n_1\,dS-\int_{S_2}J(\cdot,t)\cdot n_2\,dS=-\varepsilon_0\left(\int_{S_1}\partial_tE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_1\,dS-\int_{S_2}\partial_tE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_2\,dS\right).$$
Hence the conduction-only fluxes are equal exactly when the displacement fluxes are equal, and neither conclusion is forced by the Maxwell equations alone.

(c) [Explicit realisation] The following declared smooth data satisfies all the hypotheses above and has different conduction fluxes through the two surfaces. On $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, fix $\chi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi(z)=1$ for $z\le-1$ and $\chi(z)=0$ for $z\ge0$, and set
$$E(x,t):=\frac{t}{\varepsilon_0}\chi(z)\,e_z,\qquad B:=0,\qquad \rho(x,t):=t\,\chi'(z),\qquad J(x,t):=-\chi(z)\,e_z.$$
Then $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}B=0=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ (the last identity because $c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0$), and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. Take $D=[-1,1]^2$ and its interior $D^\circ=(-1,1)^2$. Let $\sigma$ be the standard smooth step of [[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]] and define $h(s):=\sigma(2(1-s^2))$, $\eta(u,v):=h(u)h(v)$. Then $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, $0\le\eta\le1$, $\eta=1$ in a neighbourhood of the origin, $\eta>0$ at every point of $D^\circ$, and $\eta=0$ on $\partial D$ and outside $D$. Take the graphs
$$r_1(u,v):=(u,v,-2\eta(u,v)),\qquad r_2(u,v):=(u,v,0).$$
Both induced boundary chains are the square $\{(u,v,0):(u,v)\in\partial D\}$, the region $V=\{(u,v,w):(u,v)\in D^\circ,\ -2\eta(u,v)<w<0\}$ is enclosed between the patches, and
$$\int_{S_1}J\cdot n_1\,dS=-\int_D\chi(-2\eta(u,v))\,dudv<0,\qquad \int_{S_2}J\cdot n_2\,dS=-\int_D\chi(0)\,dudv=0,$$
the first inequality because $\eta=1$ in a neighbourhood of the origin, so $\chi(-2\eta)=1$ on a nonempty open subset of $D$, whose area is positive.
while both total current fluxes in (a) vanish, consistently with the loop integral $\oint_\gamma B\cdot d\mathbf r=0$. In the standard charging-capacitor discussion the two spanning surfaces cut the conduction current in different ways and the difference is carried by the displacement term; the realisation above exhibits exactly this phenomenon in a self-contained smooth model. An idealised thin-wire current is not a source type of this framework and the capacitor interpretation is explanatory, not an additional empirical claim.
before_object.strategy: (a) Put $G:=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE$, of class $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline V$. By the smooth Gauss law and [[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], $\operatorname{div}G=\operatorname{div}J+\varepsilon_0\partial_t\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}J+\partial_t\rho=0$ on that neighbourhood, the last equality being continuity, [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]](a). [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]] applied to $G$ on the specified presentation of $V$ — outward normal $-n_1$ on the face $S_1$ and $+n_2$ on the face $S_2$ — gives $0=\int_V\operatorname{div}G=\int_{S_2}G\cdot n_2-\int_{S_1}G\cdot n_1$, which is the first asserted equality. The equality with $(1/\mu_0)\oint_\gamma B\cdot d\mathbf r$ is Ampere's integral identity of [[pthm-em-integral-maxwell]](a) applied to either patch, whose induced boundary chain is $\gamma$; the two patches consequently give the same circulation. (b) Split $G$ in the equality of (a); this is algebra with the definitions of the fluxes ([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]) and no further analytic input. (c) Verify the smooth equations for the displayed data by direct substitution: $\operatorname{div}E=(t/\varepsilon_0)\chi'(z)$ and $\operatorname{div}B=0$; $\operatorname{curl}E=\operatorname{curl}(E_z(z,t)e_z)=0$ because $E_z$ is independent of $x$ and $y$, so $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB=0$; $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ and $\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE=-\mu_0\chi(z)e_z+c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}\chi(z)e_z=0$ since $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$; and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=\chi'(z)-\chi'(z)=0$. The standard step is smooth, is zero for arguments at most zero, is one for arguments at least one and is strictly positive on $(0,1)$ ([[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]]). Thus $h$ is smooth, positive for $|s|<1$, one for $|s|\le1/\sqrt2$ and zero for $|s|\ge1$; the product $\eta$ has exactly the declared properties. In particular the entire open square has positive graph separation, rather than merely a central subregion. Both graph maps are smooth and injective regular parametrizations on a neighbourhood of $D$, since their first two coordinates are $(u,v)$ and their area vectors are $(-\varphi_u,-\varphi_v,1)$. Their induced square boundary chains coincide at height zero. The explicitly restricted $V$ is nonempty, bounded and open, with compact closure contained in $[-1,1]^2\times[-2,0]$; its boundary is exactly $S_1\cup S_2$. Strict positivity of $\eta$ on $D^\circ$ gives $S_1\cap S_2=\partial D\times\{0\}$. This square seam is a compact union of four line segments, has surface measure zero on each regular graph face, and contains the relative face boundaries. At every point off the seam the boundary is locally the single smooth graph with $V$ above the lower graph and below the upper graph. The faces therefore give the actual finite presentation of [[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]], with outward normals $-n_1,+n_2$, without overlapping positive-area face pieces. For $\varphi_1=-2\eta$, the induced upward unit normal is $n_1=(2\eta_u,2\eta_v,1)/\sqrt{1+4|\nabla\eta|^2}$, so $(J\circ r_1)\cdot n_1=-\chi(-2\eta)/\sqrt{1+4|\nabla\eta|^2}$; after multiplication by its area Jacobian the pullback density is $(J\circ r_1)\cdot(r_{1,u}\times r_{1,v})=-\chi(-2\eta)$. For the plane $n_2=e_z$ and the density is $-\chi(0)=0$. The graph flux formula thus gives exactly the two stated integrals, with the unit-normal scalar distinguished from the unnormalized area-vector density. On any ball $B(0,r)$ with $0<r<1/2$, $\eta=1$ and $\chi(-2\eta)=1$. The nonnegative continuous integrand has strictly positive integral on $D$, by the Riemann/Lebesgue comparison, monotonicity and positive ball area already declared; its negative is the strictly negative lower conduction flux, as stated. The total fluxes both vanish because $G=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE=-\chi(z)e_z+\chi(z)e_z=0$, consistent with the vanishing circulation of $B=0$. The explicit step-product supplies the required positivity on the entire square interior; the marked $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the convention of the test-geometry, surface-measure and divergence-theorem items, and no further choice is used.
